stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Linguists long assumed that young children learn new words mainly when an adult points to an object and names it for them. A study by linguist Dana Okafor, however, complicates that view. Okafor had toddlers watch two adults talk to each other. One adult used an unfamiliar word for a toy, and neither adult ever spoke to the child. Later, most of the toddlers correctly chose the toy the word referred to. This suggests that children also learn vocabulary from conversations they only overhear.
choices: To describe how a conversation between two adults was staged for a group of toddlers
To challenge the assumption that children learn new words mainly through direct naming
To argue that children learn no words when adults point to objects and name them
To confirm the view that direct naming is how children learn nearly all new words
explanation: The text opens with what linguists 'long assumed', and then 'however' signals doubt. The study shows toddlers learning a word they only overheard, which is evidence against the idea that children learn words mainly through direct naming. The text's purpose is to challenge that assumption.

A.why: You described what most of the text contains, the staged conversation, instead of what the text is for. The study is there as evidence against the old belief.

C.why: You went too far. The text says children 'also' learn from overheard speech. It never says direct naming teaches them nothing.

D.why: You missed the 'however'. The text questions the naming view. It does not confirm it.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Folklorists have often compared oral storytelling to a game of telephone, in which a tale drifts further from its original with every retelling. Yet folklorist Ilse Marten found a striking counterexample. A riddle tale written down in a coastal Norwegian parish in 1790 closely matches a version Marten recorded from a storyteller in the same parish in 2015. The two share nearly every plot event and even several exact phrases. Oral tradition, it seems, can preserve a story with surprising precision.
choices: To trace the plot events of a riddle tale told in a coastal Norwegian parish
To claim that orally transmitted tales never change as they pass between tellers
To question the view that orally transmitted tales inevitably drift from their originals
To support the idea that tales become less accurate with each new retelling
explanation: The first sentence gives a common belief, the 'game of telephone' view. 'Yet' introduces a case that cuts against it: a tale that stayed almost the same for more than two centuries. The text exists to question the idea that oral tales always drift.

A.why: You picked what the example is about rather than why it is there. The riddle tale is evidence against a belief, and the text never traces its plot.

B.why: You turned one counterexample into an absolute rule. The text says oral tradition 'can' preserve stories, not that tales never change.

D.why: You chose the belief the text argues against. 'Yet' shows the author doubts the drift view.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Marine biologists have generally regarded sea cucumbers as minor members of coral reef communities, slow animals that do little more than drift across the seafloor. Recent fieldwork by Rafael Ibarra's team suggests otherwise. On a reef where sea cucumbers had been heavily harvested, the sediment held far less oxygen than on a nearby reef where they remained plentiful. As they feed, sea cucumbers churn and aerate the sand, so their removal may harm the many organisms that live in it.
choices: To report how the sediment on one reef changed after its sea cucumbers were harvested
To argue that sea cucumbers matter more to reef health than any other reef animal
To confirm that sea cucumbers mostly drift along the seafloor with little effect on reefs
To challenge the assumption that sea cucumbers contribute little to coral reef health
explanation: The text starts with how biologists 'have generally regarded' sea cucumbers, as minor animals. 'Suggests otherwise' signals the challenge, and the sediment finding is the evidence. The text's purpose is to challenge the view that sea cucumbers matter little.

A.why: You described the finding, which takes up most of the text, instead of its job. The sediment data is there to undercut the opening belief.

B.why: You went beyond the text. It shows that sea cucumbers matter, but it never compares them to every other reef animal.

C.why: You repeated the opening belief as if the author agreed with it. 'Suggests otherwise' shows the author doubts it.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: It is often said that early mapmakers, unwilling to admit ignorance, filled unexplored regions with invented mountains, rivers, and towns. But historian Lena Voss found little support for this claim in the maps she studied. Voss examined 140 maps of inland regions made between 1750 and 1800. She found that more than half left the unexplored interiors blank, and many labeled those areas simply "unknown." For many mapmakers, Voss concludes, admitting ignorance was standard practice.
choices: To question the belief that early mapmakers routinely filled unknown areas with inventions
To describe how a historian gathered and examined a set of eighteenth-century maps
To argue that no early mapmaker ever added an invented feature to a map
To show that most eighteenth-century maps filled their interiors with invented towns
explanation: 'It is often said' introduces a common belief, and 'But' signals that the author doubts it. Voss's finding that most maps left unexplored areas blank is the evidence against it. The text's purpose is to question that belief.

B.why: You chose what the text contains, a historian studying maps, instead of what it is for. The study is evidence against the belief stated in the first sentence.

C.why: You overstated the finding. 'More than half' left areas blank, so some maps may still have included inventions. The text does not say no mapmaker ever did.

D.why: You reversed the finding. Voss found that most maps left the interiors blank rather than inventing features.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Music histories commonly suggest that the piano replaced the harpsichord soon after it was invented in the early 1700s. However, musicologist Amara Kell's survey of European concert programs paints a different picture. Of the programs from 1750 to 1790 that list a keyboard instrument, a clear majority call for a harpsichord rather than a piano. Kell argues that the older instrument remained a fixture of concert life for most of the century.
choices: To summarize the number of concert programs that called for a harpsichord after 1750
To argue that the harpsichord was more popular than the piano in every later century
To challenge the idea that the piano quickly replaced the harpsichord after its invention
To support the claim that the piano had replaced the harpsichord by the middle 1700s
explanation: The text begins with what music histories 'commonly suggest', and 'However' marks the doubt. Kell's concert program data show the harpsichord still in wide use decades later. The text exists to challenge the idea of a quick replacement.

A.why: You focused on the data rather than why it is there. The program counts are evidence against a belief, and the text gives no exact number to summarize.

B.why: You stretched the finding past its time frame. Kell's survey covers 1750 to 1790 and says nothing about later centuries.

D.why: You picked the belief the text argues against. The survey shows the harpsichord still dominant after 1750.
